title: Book of the Dead, Spell 127: Worshipping the Gods of the Orbit; said by a Person when he approaches to ... (papyrus of Iuefankh)
source: Papyrus of Iuefankh, Turin, Museo Egizio Cat. 1791 (Museo Egizio photographs, CC0) + TLA transliteration (ed. B. Backes, CC BY-SA 4.0) + English of Samuel Birch (1867, public domain)
description: Spell 127 of the Book of the Dead in the Turin papyrus of Iuefankh (Ptolemaic period): worshipping the Gods of the Orbit; said by a Person when he approaches to ..., with the TLA transliteration and Birch's 1867 English.
introduction:
The Book of the Dead, in Egyptian the spells for going forth by day, is a collection of funerary spells written on papyrus rolls and placed in burials from the New Kingdom to the Roman period. Each roll was made for one person, with spells taken from a large repertoire and illustrated with drawings (vignettes). This library gives one complete roll: the papyrus of Iuefankh in the Museo Egizio, Turin (Cat. 1791), written in the Ptolemaic period (332-30 BCE) and coming from Thebes. Richard Lepsius published it in 1842 and divided it into 165 chapters; his numbering is still the standard numbering of the spells, and it is used here.

Spell 127 (Birch: 'The book of Worshipping the Gods of the Orbit; said by a Person when he approaches to them to see that God within the Gate.') is on Lepsius's plate LI and on photograph 20 of the 31 Museo Egizio photographs of the roll.

The Egyptian is the transliteration of the Thesaurus Linguae Aegyptiae (edition by Burkhard Backes), with the column number of the spell before each column; the numbers are those of Lepsius's plates. On the papyrus the text runs in vertical columns of cursive hieroglyphs from right to left along the roll; titles and some words are written in red. Signs restored by the editor are in square brackets, signs the scribe left out in angle brackets, superfluous signs in braces and damaged signs in half brackets. The English is the translation by Samuel Birch, published in 1867 and made from Lepsius's copy of this papyrus, so the English and the Egyptian come from the same manuscript. It was the first complete English translation of the Book of the Dead; many passages are now understood differently. Birch's own square brackets give his alternatives and explanations. The photographs are by the Museo Egizio; each shows a stretch of the roll, and the note of each section says where the spell stands on it.
translator_notes: Birch's English was taken from three scans of Bunsen's Egypt's Place in Universal History, vol. V (1867), on the Internet Archive. The three OCR texts were aligned word by word and each word was settled by their agreement; running heads, page numbers, footnote markers and footnotes were removed. Some OCR errors may remain, chiefly in proper names.
Birch uses the terms and name forms of his time: Hades, Aahlu (Elysium), Tum for Atum, Seb for Geb, Anup for Anubis, Phoenix or Bennu for the heron.
Labels such as 'title line' or 'gate 1' before a line of the Egyptian translate the position labels of the TLA.
The TLA has no hieroglyphic encoding for these texts, so only the transliteration is shown.

translation.text:
CXXVII. The book of Worshipping the Gods of the Orbit; said by a Person when he approaches to them to see that God within the Gate.

Vignette. — Deceased adoring Osiris bare-headed, Sebak, and Snake-god; and three Daemon, two human, one cow-headed, with feathers on their head.]

Hail, ye Gods of the Orbit, dwelling in the West! Hail, ye Lords, keepers of the Gate! Come along, appear before Osiris, get ready, worship, strangle ye the enemies of the Sun! Shine ye, dissipate ye your darkness! Behold ye chief! live ye as he lives. Hail ye him who is in his disk! pass ye me to your road. My Soul enters your recesses, I atn one of ye. I put forth blows against the Apep [Apophis], strangle ye the wicked in the West.

Thou hast spoken truth against thy enemies, oh Great God, in his disk. Thou hast spoken truth against thy enemies, oh Osiris, Lord of the West! Thou hast spoken truth against thy enemies on heaven and earth, oh the Osiris in the South, North, West, and East. He serves Osiris who dwells in the West. He is ordered before him in the valley. He is justified before the great chiefs. He is justified in the Gate, like the shades [stars]. His Soul is as smoke against the devourer of bodies of the dead, flying over the dead, hidden from the suffocaters. Giving truth to all the created just Spirits who serve the Tasar, in all the places in which the Soul lives, adoring like the Sun, adoring like Osiris.

The deceased passes, open ye the Gates of the gateway, prepare ye his Hall when he comes. Justify ye his words against his accusers. There is given to him the food of the Gods of the Gate. There has been made for him the head attire which belongs to him, as dwelling in the hidden place, as the image of the great Waters, true Soul of a created Spirit, prevailing with his hands and arms. The Lion-Gods say to them, Very great is the deceased. They rejoice at him, they adore him, with their arms, they give to him their emblems, he has lived. The Osiris has been crowned as the living Soul of the Sun in the heaven. He has made all the appointed transformations, he has been justified before the chiefs. He has passed through the Gate on heaven and earth like the Soul of the Sun.

The deceased says: I have opened the Gate of the heaven and earth, the Soul of Osiris rests there. I cross through their Halls. They adore when they see me. go in as I like, I come out as I choose. I go along, no defect or evil is found in me.

The 31 Museo Egizio photographs (Commons p034 to p04, from the start to the end of the roll) were each compared by eye with Lepsius's plates: vignettes, red titles and framed compartments identify the spells on each photograph, and the overlapping edges of neighbouring photographs were compared side by side. Positions in the notes are measured from the left edge of the photograph.
